Even a single episode of unprotected intimacy carries two main categories of risk: pregnancy and infections that spread through intimate contact. Neither risk disappears because it was only once, or because both people felt well, or because no symptoms appeared immediately afterwards.

Regarding pregnancy: the risk depends on timing within the cycle, but since ovulation timing is not always predictable from outside, the risk is present in all cycle phases. Emergency contraception, if taken promptly, significantly reduces but does not eliminate pregnancy risk. The earlier it is taken, the more effective it is.

Regarding infections: some produce symptoms within days. Others remain silent for weeks or months while the infection continues and, in some cases, causes damage to the reproductive system. Testing after an unprotected episode, typically at around two weeks and again at three months for some infections, provides clarity that symptom-watching alone cannot.

See a doctor as early as possible after unprotected intimacy for advice about pregnancy prevention timing, what testing makes sense when, and what symptoms to watch for in the coming weeks.

When to seek help: See a doctor promptly after unprotected intimacy for guidance on pregnancy prevention, testing timeline, and which symptoms to monitor.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Which Infections Can Stay Silent Without Symptoms?
answer:
My dear,

Several infections that spread through intimate contact are known for being silent or causing very mild symptoms that are easily overlooked. Chlamydia, one of the most common, often produces no symptoms at all in women while quietly causing inflammation that can damage the fallopian tubes and affect future fertility. It can be present for months or years without the woman knowing.

Gonorrhoea in women is also frequently asymptomatic or causes only mild discharge that is attributed to normal variation. Syphilis in its early stage causes a painless ulcer that disappears on its own while the infection deepens internally. Certain strains of HPV cause no symptoms but can cause cervical changes that are only identified through regular smear testing.

This is precisely why routine sexual health testing is not only for people with symptoms. Testing provides information that symptoms alone cannot. A woman who has had any unprotected intimate contact and has not been tested recently, regardless of how she feels, cannot know her status without testing.

See a doctor for testing after any unprotected intimate contact, even without symptoms, particularly if the partner is unknown, if multiple partners are involved, or if you have not tested in the past year.

When to seek help: See a doctor for testing after unprotected intimate contact even without symptoms, as many infections are silent and detectable only through testing.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Can HIV or Other Infections Spread Through Oral or Anal Contact?
answer:
My dear,

Yes. It is a serious misconception that only one form of intimate contact carries infection risk. HIV can be transmitted through oral contact when there are sores, cuts, bleeding gums, or ulcers present in the mouth or private area. The risk of transmission through oral contact is lower than through other routes but is not zero, particularly if either person has genital sores or mouth sores from other infections.

Anal contact carries a higher risk for HIV and other infections because the tissue is more delicate and more prone to small tears during contact, providing easier entry points for viruses and bacteria. Infections including gonorrhoea, chlamydia, syphilis, herpes, and HPV can all be transmitted through anal contact. Herpes can be transmitted through close skin-to-skin contact even without penetration.

Using a condom consistently, including during oral and anal contact, and regular testing are the most effective ways to reduce these risks. Knowing the full picture of how transmission occurs empowers a woman to make informed decisions about her own protection.

See a doctor for testing after any form of intimate contact without protection, especially if there is concern about HIV or other infections, so that appropriate testing and if needed treatment can be arranged.

When to seek help: See a doctor for testing after unprotected oral or anal contact, especially if there is concern about HIV, herpes, or other infections spread through intimate contact.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: When Should I Get Tested After Risky Contact?
answer:
My dear,

The timing of testing matters because different infections become detectable at different points after exposure. Testing too early can give a false negative result, meaning the test shows no infection even though one is present, because the infection has not yet built up to detectable levels. This is called the window period.

As a general guide: tests for chlamydia and gonorrhoea are usually accurate about one to two weeks after exposure. HIV testing with modern fourth-generation tests is usually accurate at about four weeks, with confirmatory testing at three months for certainty. Syphilis testing is generally reliable at six weeks and confirmatory at three months.

Speaking to a sexual health doctor or clinic after risky contact is the best approach because they can advise on exactly which tests are appropriate given the specific type of contact, the timing, and your personal circumstances. Repeating a test at the right interval is more informative than a single early test.

See a doctor or a sexual health clinic after risky intimate contact to understand which tests are appropriate, when to take them, and what to do while waiting for results.

When to seek help: See a doctor or sexual health clinic after risky contact for guidance on which tests to take, when to take them, and what precautions are appropriate while awaiting results.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Can Condoms Fail Without Us Realising It?
answer:
My dear,

Yes. Condoms can fail in ways that are not always obvious. The most common failures are using a condom that is too old or past its expiry date, storing a condom in a wallet or car where heat and friction degrade the latex, opening the packet with teeth or sharp objects that cause small tears, putting the condom on incorrectly, and removing it before contact begins rather than throughout.

Air bubbles at the tip, which should be squeezed out before rolling on, can cause the condom to burst under pressure. Using oil-based products like body lotion, cooking oil, or petroleum jelly with latex condoms dissolves the latex and causes failure. Water-based lubricants are safe with latex. These are practical facts that are rarely taught clearly.

The failure rate of condoms used perfectly in every way is low. The real-world failure rate, which accounts for all the ways condoms are used imperfectly, is meaningfully higher. This is not a reason to abandon condoms, which are highly effective protection when used correctly. It is a reason to know how to use them correctly.

See a doctor for advice about additional protection methods if condom use feels uncertain, or after an episode where failure may have occurred.

When to seek help: See a doctor if there is concern that a condom may have failed, or for advice on additional protection methods for greater reliability.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: What Should I Do If a Condom Slips or Breaks?
answer:
My dear,

If a condom slips during or breaks during intimate contact, remain calm and take systematic action. The first step is to note the time, because the effectiveness of emergency contraception decreases significantly with each passing hour. Emergency contraception is most effective within 72 hours but can be taken up to 120 hours after unprotected contact.

If there is concern about possible exposure to an infection, particularly HIV, a doctor should be contacted as soon as possible. Post-exposure prophylaxis, PEP, a short course of medication that can prevent HIV infection from establishing, must be started within 72 hours of exposure and is most effective when started even earlier.

Write down when the exposure happened and what specifically occurred. This information helps a doctor guide the most appropriate next steps. Do not delay seeking advice out of embarrassment or the hope that nothing will come of it. Time matters in both pregnancy prevention and infection prevention.

See a doctor or emergency department as soon as possible after a condom breaks, especially within 72 hours, for emergency contraception and advice about infection risk and prevention.

When to seek help: See a doctor as soon as possible, within 72 hours, after a condom breaks for emergency contraception and assessment of infection risk.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: What Is Emergency Contraception, and When Should It Be Used?
answer:
My dear,

Emergency contraception is medication taken after unprotected intimate contact to reduce the risk of pregnancy. It is not an abortion. It works by delaying or preventing ovulation so that fertilisation is less likely to occur. It does not end an established pregnancy. This is an important distinction that often causes unnecessary fear and delay.

The most commonly available form contains levonorgestrel and is most effective when taken within 72 hours of unprotected contact, with effectiveness declining with each passing hour. Another option, ulipristal acetate, is effective up to 120 hours. A copper intrauterine device inserted within five days provides the most reliable emergency contraception available and has the added benefit of continuing as ongoing contraception.

Emergency contraception is for emergency use, not as a regular method of pregnancy prevention. If you find yourself using it repeatedly, this is a signal that a more reliable ongoing contraceptive method should be discussed with a doctor. Emergency contraception does not protect against infections.

See a doctor as soon as possible after unprotected contact, ideally within 24 hours, to receive emergency contraception at its most effective, and to discuss ongoing contraception to prevent the need for emergency measures repeatedly.

When to seek help: See a doctor as soon as possible, ideally within 24 hours, for emergency contraception, and to discuss a more reliable ongoing contraceptive if emergency contraception has been needed more than once.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Is Pain During First Intimate Closeness Normal?
answer:
My dear,

Some mild discomfort during first intimate closeness is common, but significant pain is not something that should simply be endured or accepted as inevitable. The experience of first closeness varies enormously between women. Some feel mild stretching or pressure. Some feel more significant discomfort. Some feel no pain at all. None of these responses is more correct than the others.

Significant pain during first intimacy is most commonly related to insufficient natural lubrication, which can result from anxiety, rushing, or simply not enough time for the body to prepare naturally. Anxiety activates the nervous system in ways that reduce natural lubrication and increase muscle tension, which makes discomfort more likely. This is a physiological response, not a personal failure.

If pain is very severe, if it makes closeness impossible, or if it persists after the first time, these are signs that deserve medical attention. Vaginismus, a condition where the muscles of the private area contract involuntarily, is a real and treatable cause of painful or impossible penetration that affects many women.

See a doctor if pain during first or subsequent intimate closeness is severe, persistent, or making intimacy impossible, because treatable causes exist and no woman should be left to simply endure ongoing pain.

When to seek help: See a doctor if pain during first or subsequent intimate closeness is severe, persistent, or making intimacy impossible, as treatable causes are available.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Is Bleeding the First Time Necessary?
answer:
My dear,

No, bleeding the first time is not necessary, and the absence of bleeding says nothing about a woman's character, history, or the presence or absence of a hymen. The hymen is a thin, stretchy membrane at the entrance to the private passage that varies enormously in its size, shape, and thickness between women. Many women do not bleed the first time because their hymen was naturally more elastic or had already stretched from exercise, tampons, or normal physical activity.

The belief that every woman must bleed the first time is not medically accurate and has caused tremendous unnecessary suffering, shame, anxiety, and relationship harm. It is a cultural belief, not a biological fact. A woman who does not bleed has not experienced anything abnormal. A woman who does bleed has not experienced anything that marks her as different from one who did not.

The actual physical experience of first intimacy, whether it involves brief discomfort, no discomfort, or more significant pain, depends on preparation, comfort, communication, and the pace of the experience, not on any predictable biological marker.

See a doctor if there is heavy bleeding after first intimacy, if bleeding persists for more than a day or two, or if there is significant pain that does not settle.

When to seek help: See a doctor if bleeding after first intimacy is heavy, persists beyond a day or two, or is accompanied by significant pain that does not settle.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Why Do I Feel Fear, Disgust, Panic, or Body Tightness During Closeness?
answer:
My dear,

Fear, disgust, panic, or involuntary muscle tightness during intimate closeness are real, documented experiences that affect many women and deserve compassionate understanding rather than dismissal. They can have multiple origins, and understanding the origin is the path to healing.

Vaginismus causes the muscles around the entrance to the private passage to tighten involuntarily in response to attempted penetration. The woman does not choose this. It is an automatic protective response that can develop in response to past pain, fear, trauma, or deeply held anxiety about intimacy. It is treatable with pelvic floor therapy and, where appropriate, psychological support.

Past experiences of abuse, trauma, or deeply internalised shame about the body and sexuality can create fear responses that arrive before conscious thought. These are not signs of being permanently damaged. They are signs of a mind and body that learned to protect themselves and need gentle, skilled support to learn a different response.

See a doctor or therapist if fear, panic, disgust, or involuntary tightening during intimacy is affecting your life or relationship, because appropriate support, both physical and psychological, exists and can make a significant difference.

When to seek help: See a doctor or counsellor if fear, panic, disgust, or muscle tightening during intimacy is recurring or affecting your relationship and wellbeing.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: How Do I Tell the Doctor That Closeness Is Painful or Unpleasant?
answer:
My dear,

The discomfort of telling a doctor about pain or problems with intimate closeness is real. Many women feel embarrassed, worry about being judged, or do not have the words to describe what they experience. But doctors who work in women's health have heard these concerns many times. The more clearly you can describe what is happening, the more effectively a doctor can help.

Useful information to share includes when the pain occurs, whether it is at the entrance to the private passage or deeper inside, whether it is present from the very beginning of closeness or only after some time, whether it is associated with dryness, whether it has always been present or is new, and whether it is getting better or worse over time.

You do not need to use medical words. Plain descriptions work very well. It hurts at the beginning. There is a sharp burning. There is pressure inside. I feel like my muscles tighten involuntarily. It feels like dryness and friction. All of these descriptions give a doctor meaningful, useful information.

If you find the topic impossible to discuss verbally, write down your symptoms before the appointment and hand the note to the doctor. This is a completely acceptable approach that many patients use.

When to seek help: See a doctor about pain or discomfort during intimate closeness. You can describe it in your own words or write it down. The clarity of your description helps the doctor identify and address the cause.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: What If My Spouse Asks for Acts That Hurt, Shame, or Frighten Me?
answer:
My dear,

Within any relationship, including marriage, you are entitled to say no to any act that hurts you physically, makes you feel ashamed, frightens you, or violates your sense of dignity. Consent within marriage is real and matters. A spouse asking for something you find painful, humiliating, or frightening is not a request you are obligated to fulfill.

Pain during specific acts should never be accepted as something you must endure for the sake of keeping peace or avoiding conflict. Pain is the body's signal that something is wrong. Shame and fear during intimacy that are caused by a partner's demands are not personal weaknesses. They are signals that the situation needs honest communication and, if needed, professional support.

If you are in a marriage where your right to say no is not respected, where your pain is dismissed, or where intimacy feels coercive rather than chosen, this is a serious matter that deserves support from a trusted person, a doctor, or a counsellor. You do not have to navigate it alone.

Seek support from a trusted person, doctor, or counsellor if your partner requests acts that cause you pain, shame, or fear, if your refusals are not respected, or if intimacy feels coerced rather than freely chosen.

When to seek help: Seek support from a doctor or counsellor if intimacy involves pain, shame, fear, or coercion, or if your right to refuse is not respected within the relationship.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: What Is Vaginismus, and How Is It Treated?
answer:
My dear,

Vaginismus is the name for a condition where the muscles around the entrance to the private passage contract involuntarily when penetration is attempted. The woman does not choose this contraction and cannot simply will it to stop. It is an automatic protective response of the body, and it makes penetration painful or impossible despite the woman sometimes very much wanting intimacy.

Vaginismus exists on a spectrum from mild, where penetration is possible but painful, to severe, where any attempted penetration, including a gynaecological examination, is impossible. It can affect women who have never had penetrative intimacy and women who have previously done so without difficulty.

Treatment is very effective and does not involve surgery. Pelvic floor physiotherapy, which uses exercises, progressive desensitisation, and specific techniques to help the muscles learn to relax, is the main approach. Psychological support addressing the fear and anxiety component is often highly beneficial alongside physical therapy. Many women recover completely with appropriate treatment.

See a doctor or pelvic floor physiotherapist if penetrative intimacy is painful or impossible, if pelvic examinations are very distressing, or if you recognise the pattern of involuntary muscle tightening described here.

When to seek help: See a doctor or pelvic floor physiotherapist if intimacy is painful or impossible due to involuntary muscle tightening, as effective treatment is available.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: How Does Past Trauma Affect Intimate Life in Marriage?
answer:
My dear,

Experiences of abuse, assault, or other intimate trauma leave marks on the nervous system that can show up in intimate life months or years later, often in ways that are confusing and distressing to the woman herself. A smell, a specific touch, a particular position, or even a feeling of vulnerability during closeness can trigger a fear response that seems to arrive from nowhere.

These triggers are not signs of weakness or permanent damage. They are the nervous system faithfully doing what it learned to do: protect against a previously experienced threat. The challenge is that the current situation is safe, but the body does not yet fully know this.

Healing from trauma's effects on intimate life usually benefits from a combination of psychological support, specifically trauma-informed therapy, and in some cases pelvic floor physiotherapy if physical symptoms are present. Partner patience and communication also matter significantly. Recovery is possible for most women with appropriate, compassionate support.

Seek help from a trauma-informed therapist or doctor if past trauma is affecting your current intimate life, causing fear, panic, flashbacks, avoidance, or body tightening during closeness.

When to seek help: Seek help from a trauma-informed therapist or doctor if past trauma is creating fear, avoidance, flashbacks, or physical symptoms during intimate closeness.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: When Do Pain and Fear Need Both Medical and Counselling Help?
answer:
My dear,

Painful closeness is often not purely physical, and fear during intimacy is often not purely psychological. The two are deeply connected and often reinforce each other. Physical pain creates fear of future pain. Fear creates muscle tension that causes more pain. This cycle can continue for years without either aspect being addressed fully.

A doctor can investigate and treat physical causes: skin conditions, infections, hormone-related dryness, vaginismus, endometriosis with deep pain, and pelvic floor dysfunction. A counsellor or therapist can address the fear, anxiety, shame, communication difficulties, and any trauma history that contributes to the experience.

When treatment of the physical cause alone does not fully resolve the problem, or when fear or avoidance are significantly present, combined support produces the best outcomes. Both aspects of the problem deserve simultaneous attention, not one after the other.

Seek combined medical and counselling support if pain, fear, dryness, or muscle tightening during intimate closeness persists despite physical treatment, or if emotional and psychological factors are clearly part of the picture.

When to seek help: Seek combined medical and counselling help if physical treatment alone has not resolved pain or fear during intimate closeness, or if both physical and emotional factors are contributing.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Why Do I Leak Urine When I Cough, Laugh, Sneeze, or Run?
category: Bladder, Urine, and Pelvic Floor Problems
answer:
My dear,

Leaking urine when pressure suddenly rises inside the abdomen, during coughing, laughing, sneezing, lifting, or running, is called stress urinary incontinence. It happens when the pelvic floor muscles and the bladder outlet are not holding firmly enough against that sudden increase in pressure. A small amount of urine escapes before the woman can stop it.

This affects a very large number of women and is strongly associated with childbirth, particularly vaginal delivery, but it also affects women who have never given birth and women of all ages. It is not a normal price to pay for having had children, and it is not simply a sign of ageing that must be accepted.

Pelvic floor physiotherapy, which involves specific exercises for the muscles that support the bladder, uterus, and bowel, is the evidence-based first-line treatment. When done correctly and consistently, it produces significant improvement or complete resolution in the majority of women. Generic advice to do Kegel exercises alone, without proper guidance on technique, is less effective than physiotherapy-guided training.

See a doctor or pelvic floor physiotherapist if leakage is frequent, worsening, affecting your activities, causing embarrassment, or following childbirth, as effective treatment is available and no woman needs to simply accept this condition.

When to seek help: See a doctor or pelvic floor physiotherapist if leakage is frequent, worsening, or affecting your daily activities, as effective treatment can produce significant or complete improvement.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Why Do I Suddenly Feel a Strong Need to Pass Urine That I Cannot Hold?
category: Bladder, Urine, and Pelvic Floor Problems
answer:
My dear,

A sudden, intense, difficult-to-defer urge to pass urine, sometimes resulting in leakage before reaching the toilet, describes what is called urgency urinary incontinence or overactive bladder. The bladder sends an urgent signal before it is actually full. The urge arrives with little warning and feels impossible to ignore.

This condition affects many women and leads to significant changes in behaviour, planning life around the location of toilets, reducing fluid intake, avoiding long journeys, and limiting social activities. These adaptations are understandable but often worsen the situation by making the bladder more sensitive to small volumes.

Reducing caffeine and alcohol, which are bladder irritants, maintaining adequate but not excessive fluid intake, bladder training exercises that gradually extend the time between urges, and pelvic floor work are all effective first approaches. Medication is available for more significant cases. The condition is treatable, and treating it meaningfully improves quality of life.

See a doctor if urgency is frequent, causes leakage, disturbs your sleep, limits your activities, or is accompanied by burning, fever, or blood in the urine.

When to seek help: See a doctor if urgency is frequent, causing leakage, disturbing sleep, or limiting activities, as effective treatments including bladder training and medication are available.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Why Do I Have Burning Urine Even When My Reports Look Normal?
category: Bladder, Urine, and Pelvic Floor Problems
answer:
My dear,

Burning on passing urine without a urine infection is a confusing and frustrating experience that many women encounter. The key to understanding it lies in recognising that the burning sensation does not always originate inside the bladder. Urine passing over skin that is already irritated, inflamed, dry, or damaged outside the urethra causes exactly the same stinging sensation as a bladder infection.

Skin conditions of the private area, including contact allergy, fungal infection, bacterial imbalance, lichen sclerosus, or herpes sores, can all cause burning when urine touches them. Dehydration, causing very concentrated urine, can irritate the urethral lining even without infection. Small kidney stones passing through the urinary system cause burning as they move.

A normal urine culture does not mean the symptom is imaginary or exaggerated. It means the cause lies somewhere other than a bacterial bladder infection. Broadening the evaluation to include the skin of the private area, hydration, possible kidney stone assessment, and bladder sensitivity usually identifies the actual cause.

See a doctor if burning on urination persists despite normal urine reports, or if it comes with visible skin changes, discharge, frequency, blood in urine, or lower back pain.

When to seek help: See a doctor if burning on urination persists with normal urine reports, or if accompanied by skin changes, discharge, blood in urine, or back pain.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Why Do I Get Repeated Urine Infections After Intimate Closeness?
category: Bladder, Urine, and Pelvic Floor Problems
answer:
My dear,

Post-coital urinary tract infections, colloquially known as honeymoon cystitis, occur because intimate contact can push bacteria from the surrounding skin into the short female urethra, where they ascend to the bladder. Women are more prone to this than men because the female urethra is shorter and the urethral opening is closer to the sources of bacteria.

Habits that reduce this risk include passing urine promptly after intimate contact, which flushes bacteria from the urethra before they establish; staying well hydrated so that urine volume is adequate for regular flushing; and ensuring good hygiene without excessive washing that strips the natural protective environment.

For women with a clear established pattern of infection after intimacy, a doctor may prescribe a low-dose antibiotic taken specifically after intimate contact, which has been shown to effectively prevent recurrence. This is a targeted, evidence-based approach that avoids the need for frequent full antibiotic courses.

See a doctor if urine infections repeatedly follow intimate contact, if they come with fever or back pain, or if they require repeated antibiotics without a lasting solution, as a preventive strategy may be appropriate.

When to seek help: See a doctor if urine infections repeatedly follow intimacy, come with fever or back pain, or require repeated antibiotics, as a preventive antibiotic strategy may be appropriate.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Why Do I Pass Urine Frequently Even Without Infection?
category: Bladder, Urine, and Pelvic Floor Problems
answer:
My dear,

Frequent urination without infection has several possible causes. Diabetes is one of the most important to consider, as high blood sugar causes the kidneys to produce more urine to excrete the excess glucose, leading to increased frequency and volume. Excessive fluid intake, particularly of caffeine-containing drinks, is a very common and simple cause that is often overlooked.

An overactive bladder, where the bladder sends signals of urgency before it is appropriately full, causes frequency without any infectious cause. Anxiety is a recognised trigger for increased urinary frequency. Pregnancy, pelvic organ prolapse, and certain medicines can all cause frequency as well.

The body is not sending random signals. Understanding the pattern, whether frequency is high throughout the day or only at certain times, whether it accompanies increased thirst or other symptoms, and whether small or large amounts are passed each time, helps identify the cause accurately.

See a doctor if frequency is new, progressively worsening, disturbing sleep, accompanied by thirst, weight change, urgency, or leakage, or if it is significantly affecting your daily routine.

When to seek help: See a doctor if frequency is new, worsening, accompanied by thirst, weight change, urgency, or leakage, or if it is disrupting sleep or daily activities.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: What Is Pelvic Organ Prolapse, and Why Does It Happen?
category: Bladder, Urine, and Pelvic Floor Problems
answer:
My dear,

Pelvic organ prolapse occurs when the muscles and connective tissue that support the uterus, bladder, or bowel weaken or stretch, allowing one or more of these organs to shift downward toward or into the private passage. Women describe it as a feeling of heaviness, pressure, or the sensation of something coming down or out below.

Vaginal childbirth, particularly multiple deliveries or deliveries involving large babies or assisted delivery, is the most common cause. The pelvic floor tissue stretches significantly during delivery and may not fully recover its previous strength. Menopause reduces the oestrogen that helps maintain the strength and elasticity of these tissues. Chronic constipation, heavy lifting, chronic cough, and obesity all increase the pressure on pelvic supports over time.

Many women live with significant prolapse for years without knowing that effective treatment exists. They accept the heaviness and discomfort as an inevitable consequence of childbirth or ageing. Pelvic floor physiotherapy, supportive devices called ring pessaries, and surgical repair are all available options depending on the severity and the woman's preferences.

See a doctor if you feel heaviness or pressure below, a sensation of something bulging out, difficulty fully emptying the bladder or bowel, or urinary leakage alongside pelvic discomfort.

When to seek help: See a doctor if you feel heaviness or pressure in the pelvic area, a sensation of something coming down, or difficulty emptying the bladder or bowel, as effective treatments are available.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Why Do I Feel Pelvic Pressure or Pain After Standing Too Long?
category: Bladder, Urine, and Pelvic Floor Problems
answer:
My dear,

Pelvic pressure or pain that worsens after prolonged standing, walking, or physical activity and improves with lying down or rest is a recognisable pattern associated with pelvic organ prolapse. When the supporting structures are weakened, the weight of the pelvic organs, especially when gravity is working against weakened supports throughout a long day, creates a progressive sense of heaviness and discomfort.

This symptom is particularly common towards the end of the day after several hours on your feet. Women often report that they feel mostly comfortable in the morning and progressively more uncomfortable as the day continues. Some describe it as feeling like something is pressing down or about to fall out, which understandably causes anxiety.

A well-fitting ring pessary, which is a supportive device placed inside the private passage to hold the organs in a better position, can provide excellent and immediate symptom relief for many women. Pelvic floor exercises strengthen the supporting muscles and can reduce symptoms over weeks to months of consistent practice.

See a doctor if pelvic pressure or a sensation of heaviness is worsening, affecting your daily activities, or accompanied by any bulging that can be felt or seen at the opening of the private passage.

When to seek help: See a doctor if pelvic pressure or heaviness is worsening, affecting daily activities, or accompanied by any visible or palpable bulging at the vaginal opening.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Why Do I Have Painful Periods That Also Cause Bowel Problems?
category: Bladder, Urine, and Pelvic Floor Problems
answer:
My dear,

Period pain that is also accompanied by pain when opening the bowels, diarrhoea or constipation specifically around the time of periods, or blood in the stool during periods is a pattern that often points toward endometriosis affecting the bowel or the tissue between the uterus and bowel.

Endometriosis, a condition where tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus, can implant on the bowel, causing inflammation and pain that follows the menstrual cycle. Because the implants respond to the same hormones as the uterine lining, they swell and bleed during each period, causing local pain and bowel symptoms.

Many women with bowel-related period symptoms have seen multiple doctors over years without receiving the diagnosis of endometriosis because the connection between the two symptom sets is not always recognised. If your bowel symptoms are clearly cycle-related, appearing or significantly worsening with each period, this connection is worth raising explicitly with a gynaecologist.

See a gynaecologist if bowel symptoms including pain, diarrhoea, constipation, or bleeding reliably coincide with your period or with ovulation, and mention the cyclical pattern specifically.

When to seek help: See a gynaecologist if painful bowel symptoms reliably occur with each period or around ovulation, as this pattern may indicate endometriosis affecting the bowel.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Can I Have a Baby After Repeated Pelvic Infections?
category: Bladder, Urine, and Pelvic Floor Problems
answer:
My dear,

Pelvic inflammatory disease, PID, is an infection of the uterus and fallopian tubes that can cause scarring if not treated promptly and completely. Each episode of PID increases the risk of tubal damage, and repeated episodes carry a higher cumulative risk of affecting fertility than a single treated episode. This is not inevitable, but it is a genuine consideration.

The good news is that one treated episode of PID does not necessarily affect fertility significantly if treatment was prompt and complete. Many women conceive naturally after PID. The key factors are how early treatment was started, whether it was completed, how many episodes occurred, and whether there were any complications.

If you have had PID and are planning a pregnancy, discussing your history with a gynaecologist before trying to conceive is sensible. This allows appropriate assessment of tubal health if any concerns exist and enables early support if conception is slower than expected.

See a doctor before trying to conceive if you have a history of pelvic inflammatory disease, repeated infections, or prior treatment for fertility problems, so that appropriate assessment and support can be offered.

When to seek help: See a doctor before trying to conceive if you have a history of pelvic infections, as assessment of tubal health may be appropriate and early support can be arranged if needed.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: What Is Pelvic Floor Physiotherapy and Who Needs It?
category: Bladder, Urine, and Pelvic Floor Problems
answer:
My dear,

The pelvic floor is a group of muscles arranged like a hammock at the base of the pelvis, supporting the uterus, bladder, and bowel. When these muscles are weakened or too tight, or when their coordination is poor, a range of symptoms can result including urinary leakage, urgency, pelvic prolapse, pelvic pain, and painful intimate closeness.

Pelvic floor physiotherapy is a specialised form of physiotherapy conducted by therapists trained specifically in assessment and treatment of these muscles. It involves both internal and external examination techniques, specific exercise programmes tailored to whether the muscles need strengthening or relaxation, biofeedback, and education about the pelvic floor as a system.

Almost every woman who has given birth vaginally benefits from pelvic floor assessment, even if she has no current symptoms, because pelvic floor changes after delivery are common and prevention of future problems is easier than treating established ones. Women with urinary leakage, pelvic pressure, painful intimacy, and pelvic pain all benefit from this specialised support.

Ask your doctor for a referral to a pelvic floor physiotherapist if you have urinary leakage, pelvic pressure, painful intimacy, pelvic pain, or any history of difficult vaginal delivery.

When to seek help: Ask your doctor for a referral to a pelvic floor physiotherapist if you have urinary leakage, pelvic pressure or prolapse, painful intimate closeness, or a history of challenging vaginal delivery.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: How Long Is It Normal to Try Before Becoming Pregnant?
answer:
My dear,

For couples trying to conceive without any contraception and having regular intimate contact, it is completely normal for conception to take up to twelve months. Statistics show that about 85 percent of couples conceive within one year of trying. The remaining 15 percent take longer and are referred for fertility assessment, but many go on to conceive naturally or with modest assistance.

Age matters significantly. Women under 35 are generally advised to try for twelve months before seeking assessment. Women between 35 and 40 are advised to seek assessment after six months. Women over 40, or those with known risk factors for fertility difficulties, such as very irregular or absent periods, a history of pelvic infection, or known conditions like PCOS or endometriosis, may benefit from earlier assessment.

The emotional difficulty of trying and waiting should not be underestimated. Monthly hope followed by monthly disappointment is genuinely painful, and this pain is real and valid. It deserves acknowledgement alongside practical medical guidance.

See a doctor after twelve months of trying without conception if under 35, after six months if between 35 and 40, or sooner if there are known risk factors, very irregular cycles, previous pelvic infections, or significant anxiety about fertility.

When to seek help: See a doctor after 12 months of trying if under 35, after 6 months if 35 to 40, or sooner if there are irregular cycles, previous infections, or other known risk factors.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: What Is Ovulation and How Do I Know If It Is Happening?
answer:
My dear,

Ovulation is the release of a mature egg from the ovary, which typically occurs once per cycle, around the middle of the cycle in a regular 28-day pattern, though the exact timing varies considerably between women and from cycle to cycle. Ovulation is the essential event that makes conception possible, and cycles without ovulation are called anovulatory cycles.

Several signs can suggest that ovulation is occurring: a clear, stretchy, egg-white-like discharge around mid-cycle, a slight rise in basal body temperature after ovulation, mild one-sided pelvic twinging called mittelschmerz, and, most reliably, a regular monthly period arriving approximately fourteen days after ovulation. Ovulation predictor kits available in pharmacies detect the hormone surge that precedes ovulation.

Women with irregular or infrequent periods may not be ovulating regularly, and this is one of the most common causes of difficulty conceiving. If periods are irregular, a simple blood test can help determine whether ovulation is occurring and what might be causing it to be absent or irregular.

See a doctor if periods are irregular or infrequent and you are trying to conceive, if you have been trying for the recommended time without success, or if you want guidance on identifying your fertile window.

When to seek help: See a doctor if periods are irregular, you have been trying to conceive without success, or you want guidance on identifying when ovulation is occurring.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: What Are the Tests for Female Fertility?
answer:
My dear,

Fertility assessment in women begins with understanding the full picture: a detailed history of the menstrual cycle, any previous pregnancies or losses, pelvic infections, medical conditions, medicines, surgical history, and lifestyle factors including weight, smoking, alcohol, and stress.

Blood tests typically include hormone levels at specific cycle days, including follicle stimulating hormone and anti-Mullerian hormone which reflect ovarian reserve, progesterone mid-cycle which confirms ovulation occurred, thyroid function, and prolactin. An ultrasound scan examines the uterus, ovaries, and the number of developing follicles visible.

If tubal assessment is needed, a procedure called a hysterosalpingogram, HSG, or similar test, can show whether the fallopian tubes are open. Evaluation is most useful when both partners are assessed together, because male factors contribute to difficulty conceiving in approximately half of cases.

See a fertility doctor or gynaecologist for assessment after trying to conceive for the recommended period, or earlier if there are known risk factors, and discuss whether both partners should be assessed together.

When to seek help: See a doctor for fertility assessment after trying for the recommended period, and request that both partners be assessed, as male factors contribute to difficulty conceiving in a significant proportion of cases.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Is PCOS a Cause of Infertility?
answer:
My dear,

Polycystic ovary syndrome is the most common hormonal cause of female infertility, but it is important to understand what this actually means. PCOS does not prevent most women from ever conceiving. It interferes with ovulation, meaning eggs are released less regularly or less predictably, which makes conception harder rather than impossible.

Many women with PCOS conceive naturally. Many others conceive with relatively simple support such as lifestyle changes that improve insulin sensitivity, weight normalisation where relevant, or ovulation induction, which is medication that helps trigger regular egg release. More complex fertility treatment is needed for a smaller proportion.

The positive framing of PCOS and fertility is important: most women with PCOS who want to conceive, do conceive, often with support. Receiving the diagnosis is not a sentence of childlessness. It is information that allows targeted, effective care to be provided.

See a fertility specialist if you have PCOS and are trying to conceive, as effective ovulation induction strategies are available that significantly improve the chance of natural conception.

When to seek help: See a doctor or fertility specialist if you have PCOS and are trying to conceive, as ovulation induction and other interventions are effective and available.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: What Is Egg Reserve and Does It Affect Fertility?
answer:
My dear,

Ovarian reserve refers to the number and quality of eggs remaining in the ovaries. Women are born with all the eggs they will ever have, and unlike men who produce new sperm throughout their lives, the egg supply declines with age. This decline becomes more significant from the mid-thirties onwards and accelerates further in the forties.

Anti-Mullerian hormone, AMH, is a blood test that reflects the size of the remaining egg pool. A lower AMH suggests fewer eggs remaining. It does not directly predict whether a woman will conceive, but it helps guide the urgency and approach of fertility treatment if needed. An ultrasound count of small follicles, called the antral follicle count, provides similar information.

Women with low ovarian reserve may still conceive naturally or with fertility treatment, but they may have less time to try before egg quality becomes a limiting factor. Understanding this allows informed decisions about the pace of investigation and treatment rather than discovering the situation urgently when time is shortest.

See a doctor for ovarian reserve testing if you are over 35 and planning a family, if you have had ovarian surgery, if you have a family history of early menopause, or if you have been trying to conceive for more than six months.

When to seek help: See a doctor for ovarian reserve assessment if over 35 and planning a pregnancy, after ovarian surgery, with a family history of early menopause, or if trying to conceive for more than six months.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Can Thyroid Problems Affect My Ability to Conceive?
answer:
My dear,

Yes, significantly. The thyroid gland affects almost every system in the body, and reproductive function is particularly sensitive to thyroid hormone levels. Both underactive thyroid, hypothyroidism, and overactive thyroid, hyperthyroidism, can interfere with ovulation, cycle regularity, and the ability to maintain a pregnancy.

Subclinical hypothyroidism, where TSH is mildly elevated but the woman has no obvious symptoms, is associated with increased risk of miscarriage and difficulty conceiving. Thyroid antibodies, even when hormone levels appear normal, may also be associated with reproductive difficulties in some women.

Checking thyroid function is a simple blood test that is routinely included in fertility assessment. If a thyroid problem is found, treatment is straightforward, effective, and safe in pregnancy. Correcting thyroid function before conceiving reduces the risk of early pregnancy loss and supports healthy pregnancy development.

See a doctor for thyroid testing if you are trying to conceive, have irregular periods, have experienced early pregnancy losses, have fatigue or weight changes, or have not had thyroid function checked recently.

When to seek help: See a doctor for thyroid testing if trying to conceive, especially with irregular periods, previous pregnancy losses, fatigue, or weight change, as thyroid correction significantly improves conception and pregnancy outcomes.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Can Lifestyle Factors Reduce Fertility?
answer:
My dear,

Yes. Fertility is influenced by the whole body's health, not only the reproductive organs in isolation. Smoking damages egg quality, disrupts hormone balance, affects blood flow to the uterus, and is associated with earlier menopause. The effects of smoking on fertility are well-documented and stopping smoking is one of the most impactful changes a woman planning pregnancy can make.

Alcohol in significant quantities disrupts hormones, liver function, and the hormonal signals that govern ovulation. Very high body weight, through insulin resistance and hormone disruption, reduces the regularity of ovulation. Very low body weight or excessive exercise can suppress the brain's hormonal signals to the ovaries entirely, stopping ovulation completely.

Chronic significant stress activates hormone pathways that can suppress the reproductive hormonal signal chain. Sleep deprivation disrupts the hormonal patterns that are needed for regular ovulation. These effects are not theoretical. They are measurable, real, and reversible with appropriate changes.

See a doctor if lifestyle factors including smoking, significant weight change, very intense exercise, or chronic high stress are present alongside difficulty conceiving, as addressing these may improve the chance of natural conception significantly.

When to seek help: See a doctor if lifestyle factors such as smoking, significant weight change, excessive exercise, or chronic stress are present alongside difficulty conceiving.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Can My Husband's Health Also Affect Infertility?
answer:
My dear,

Yes, very significantly. Male factors contribute to difficulty conceiving in approximately half of couples who seek fertility assessment. This means that focusing only on the woman when a couple is having difficulty conceiving misses a very large proportion of the actual causes. Both partners deserve evaluation.

Male fertility is affected by sperm count, the percentage of sperm that move normally, and the shape of sperm. Conditions including diabetes, high blood pressure, certain infections including mumps after puberty, varicoceles, hormone problems, and certain medicines can all affect sperm. Lifestyle factors including smoking, excessive alcohol, obesity, and heat exposure to the testicles from tight underwear or prolonged sitting also affect sperm quality.

A semen analysis is a simple, non-invasive test that gives a great deal of information about male fertility. It is not a test of masculinity or virility. It is a medical measurement, like any other, that helps understand a couple's situation accurately and plan the most effective support.

Seek fertility assessment as a couple, ensuring the male partner is also evaluated with a semen analysis, as male factors are involved in approximately half of all cases of difficulty conceiving.

When to seek help: Seek fertility assessment as a couple with both partners evaluated, as male factors contribute to approximately half of all cases of difficulty conceiving.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: What Are the Earliest Signs of Pregnancy?
answer:
My dear,

The earliest signs of pregnancy vary between women and even between pregnancies in the same woman. A missed period in a woman with regular cycles is often the most obvious first clue. Some women notice early signs even before the period is missed: unusual fatigue, breast heaviness or tenderness, mild nausea, more frequent urination, increased sleepiness, or a subtle change in how food smells or tastes.

Light spotting around the time of implantation, when the fertilised egg settles into the uterine lining, occurs in some women and can be confused with a very light period. A lower tummy pulling sensation, emotional sensitivity, and simply feeling "different" in a way that is hard to describe are also reported by some women in very early pregnancy.

An early pregnancy test using first morning urine, which is the most concentrated, can detect pregnancy from the day of a missed period or sometimes a day or two before in some tests. A positive test is reliable. A negative test in a woman with a missed period but clear symptoms is worth repeating a few days later.

See a doctor if a period is missed and a test is positive, if there is unusual lower abdominal pain with a possible pregnancy, if bleeding accompanies a positive test, or if you need guidance about early pregnancy care.

When to seek help: See a doctor if a period is missed and a test is positive, if there is lower abdominal pain with pregnancy, if bleeding accompanies a positive test, or for guidance on early pregnancy care.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: When Is Bleeding in Early Pregnancy Dangerous?
answer:
My dear,

Any bleeding in early pregnancy should be taken seriously, even though not all early pregnancy bleeding ends in loss. Light spotting without pain in very early pregnancy, called implantation bleeding, can be normal. But any bleeding that is heavier than a light spotting, or that is accompanied by lower abdominal pain, cramps, dizziness, shoulder tip pain, or feeling faint, requires urgent medical assessment.

An ectopic pregnancy, where the embryo implants outside the uterus, usually in the fallopian tube, is a medical emergency. The classic warning signs are lower abdominal pain on one side, shoulder tip pain from internal bleeding irritating the diaphragm, dizziness, and faintness. Some women have very little or no vaginal bleeding. Ectopic pregnancy can be life-threatening if not identified and treated promptly.

A threatened miscarriage, where bleeding occurs but the pregnancy continues, and an incomplete or complete miscarriage, where the pregnancy is ending, are managed differently and require different care. An ultrasound scan with a doctor's assessment determines which situation is present.

Go to the emergency department or see a doctor urgently if early pregnancy is accompanied by more than light spotting, or by any pain, dizziness, shoulder pain, or faintness. Do not wait to see if it settles.

When to seek help: Go to the emergency department urgently if early pregnancy bleeding is more than light spotting, or if it is accompanied by pain, dizziness, shoulder pain, or faintness.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Why Does Miscarriage Happen? Is It the Woman's Fault?
answer:
My dear,

No. Miscarriage is almost never the woman's fault. The majority of early miscarriages occur because the embryo did not develop a chromosomally normal set of cells during the very early cell divisions. The body recognises this and naturally ends a pregnancy that could not continue to a healthy birth. This process is the body working correctly, not failing.

Women frequently blame themselves, reviewing everything they ate, every journey they took, every heavy thing they lifted, every argument they had, looking for the action that caused the loss. In the vast majority of cases, none of these things were the cause, and the loss would have occurred regardless.

Miscarriage can sometimes be related to identifiable causes including significant thyroid imbalance, antiphospholipid syndrome, structural problems with the uterus, or chromosomal issues in the parents. These are medical factors, not personal failures. They are identifiable and in many cases treatable.

Grief after miscarriage is real, significant, and deserves acknowledgement and space. If you are struggling with grief, guilt, fear, or the emotional impact of pregnancy loss, please speak to a doctor or counsellor. Your pain matters.

When to seek help: See a doctor or counsellor if you are struggling with grief, guilt, or fear after miscarriage, and see a doctor for investigation if you have had two or more miscarriages.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: How Long Should We Wait After Miscarriage Before Trying Again?
answer:
My dear,

There is no single universally recommended waiting period that applies to every woman after every miscarriage. Physical recovery depends on how far the pregnancy had progressed, how the loss occurred, whether any treatment was needed, and whether any anaemia or weakness remains. Many doctors have traditionally suggested waiting for one normal period before trying again, which allows a clear dating point for the next pregnancy.

Emotional readiness is equally important and follows a different timeline for different women. Some feel ready to try again relatively quickly as part of processing the grief and moving forward. Others need months before the prospect of another pregnancy does not feel terrifying. Neither response is wrong.

If the cause of the miscarriage has been investigated and an addressable factor found, correcting that factor before the next pregnancy rather than trying immediately makes biological sense. There is no evidence that trying quickly after a miscarriage worsens outcomes in most situations.

See a doctor before trying again if the miscarriage was the second or third, if an investigation was recommended, if bleeding lasted longer than expected, or if you feel physically or emotionally unready.

When to seek help: See a doctor before trying again if it was a second or subsequent miscarriage, if investigation was recommended, or if physical or emotional recovery is incomplete.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: What Tests Are Needed After Repeated Miscarriages?
answer:
My dear,

After two or more pregnancy losses, a thorough investigation is recommended to identify any treatable underlying causes. The specific tests depend on each woman's history, age, and the pattern of losses, but a standard panel typically includes hormone levels including thyroid, investigation for antiphospholipid syndrome which causes blood clotting that can interrupt pregnancy, an ultrasound of the uterus to check its shape, and chromosomal analysis of both partners.

Antiphospholipid syndrome is one of the most important and most treatable causes of recurrent miscarriage. When identified, treatment with low-dose aspirin and sometimes a blood-thinning injection during pregnancy dramatically improves the chance of a successful pregnancy. This is a condition worth testing for in any woman with two or more losses.

Not every test identifies a cause, and for a proportion of women with recurrent loss, no underlying cause is found. This is profoundly frustrating. However, the chance of a successful next pregnancy with specialist monitoring is still high even when no cause is identified.

See a doctor or recurrent miscarriage specialist after two or more pregnancy losses to discuss which investigations are appropriate for your specific situation.

When to seek help: See a recurrent miscarriage specialist or gynaecologist after two or more pregnancy losses to arrange appropriate investigation, particularly for antiphospholipid syndrome.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: What Is an Ectopic Pregnancy and Why Is It Dangerous?
answer:
My dear,

An ectopic pregnancy occurs when the fertilised egg implants and begins to grow outside the uterine cavity, most commonly in the fallopian tube. Unlike the uterus, the fallopian tube cannot expand to accommodate a growing pregnancy. As the pregnancy grows, it stretches and can rupture the tube, causing internal bleeding that is life-threatening.

The risk of ectopic pregnancy is higher in women with a history of pelvic inflammatory disease or STIs that may have caused tubal scarring, previous ectopic pregnancy, previous pelvic or tubal surgery, IUD use, and endometriosis. However, ectopic pregnancy can occur in women with no identifiable risk factors.

Early symptoms include lower abdominal pain, often on one side, that may be mild at first and worsen with time. Vaginal bleeding may or may not be present. Shoulder tip pain from blood irritating the diaphragm, dizziness, and faintness indicate internal bleeding and represent a medical emergency requiring immediate hospital attendance.

Go to the emergency department immediately if you have a positive or possible pregnancy alongside one-sided lower abdominal pain, dizziness, shoulder tip pain, or faintness. This combination cannot wait.

When to seek help: Go to the emergency department immediately if you have a positive pregnancy test and one-sided pelvic pain, shoulder tip pain, dizziness, or faintness, as ectopic pregnancy is a medical emergency.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: How Is Pregnancy Confirmed and Dated Accurately?
answer:
My dear,

A positive urine pregnancy test is reliable from around the time of a missed period. Blood pregnancy tests can detect the pregnancy hormone slightly earlier. Once a positive test is obtained, an ultrasound scan between six and twelve weeks gestation is the most accurate way to confirm that the pregnancy is developing in the correct location, to assess the heartbeat, and to establish an accurate due date.

Dating the pregnancy accurately matters for many reasons: it guides screening test timing, it provides the due date that helps identify when the baby is overdue, it allows appropriate monitoring, and it gives parents a clear timeline. Dating by the last menstrual period alone can be inaccurate if cycles are irregular or if the remembered date is uncertain.

The due date calculated at the dating scan is the most reliable guide. It does not mean the baby will arrive on that exact day; only about five percent of babies are born on their exact due date. But it provides the landmark from which all subsequent assessments are timed.

See a doctor as soon as a pregnancy test is positive to arrange early pregnancy care, confirm the location of the pregnancy, and schedule appropriate early scans and assessments.

When to seek help: See a doctor as soon as a pregnancy test is positive to arrange early pregnancy care and early scan to confirm location, assess the pregnancy, and establish an accurate due date.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: What Happens to My Body During Normal Labour?
answer:
My dear,

Labour is the process through which the uterus contracts rhythmically and progressively to open the cervix and eventually push the baby out. It is divided into three stages: the first stage is when contractions gradually open the cervix from closed to fully open, which is the longest part of labour. The second stage is when the fully open cervix allows the baby to be pushed down and born. The third stage is the delivery of the placenta.

Early contractions may feel like period cramps or back pain and are often irregular and mild. As labour progresses, contractions become stronger, longer, and more regular, eventually coming every two to five minutes and lasting about a minute each. This is the pattern that indicates active labour.

Pain in labour is real and significant. Every woman experiences and copes with it differently. Options for pain relief range from breathing techniques, water immersion, and movement, to entonox gas, injections, and epidural anaesthesia. There is no right or wrong way to manage labour pain. The goal is comfort, safety, and a positive experience.

Contact your maternity team when contractions are regular and progressing, when your waters break, when you have any bleeding, when you feel the baby is not moving as usual, or when you are uncertain and want to be assessed.

When to seek help: Contact your maternity team when contractions are regular and five minutes apart, when waters break, when bleeding occurs, when baby movements reduce, or when you want reassurance.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: What Is an Episiotomy, and Why Might It Be Needed?
answer:
My dear,

An episiotomy is a small surgical cut made in the tissue between the vaginal opening and the anus during delivery to enlarge the opening and allow the baby to be born more easily. It is made with scissors under local anaesthetic and is repaired with stitches after delivery.

Episiotomy is not performed routinely in all deliveries. It is considered when the baby needs to be born quickly for safety reasons, when the baby's shoulders are becoming stuck, when a forceps or ventouse delivery is being performed, or when the tissue is about to tear in a direction that would be more harmful than a controlled cut.

The stitches after an episiotomy dissolve on their own over several weeks. The area can be sore for days to weeks. Good hygiene, adequate pain relief, and pelvic floor exercises to support healing all contribute to recovery. Persistent pain beyond a few weeks, signs of infection, or concerns about healing all deserve medical review.

See a doctor if episiotomy pain is severe and not reducing, if there are signs of infection such as increasing redness, swelling, or discharge, if the wound appears to be opening, or if pain is affecting your recovery and daily care.

When to seek help: See a doctor if episiotomy pain is severe, not reducing, showing signs of infection, or if the wound is not healing normally.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Why Do I Still Feel Pain Weeks After Delivery?
answer:
My dear,

Some discomfort in the first weeks after delivery is expected and normal. The uterus contracts as it returns to its pre-pregnancy size, causing afterpains that can be quite strong, particularly during breastfeeding when oxytocin stimulates uterine contraction. The perineum, whether from a natural tear or an episiotomy, is sore and tender as it heals.

Pain that is severe, increasing rather than decreasing, or accompanied by fever, foul-smelling discharge, difficulty passing urine, or feeling generally unwell may indicate an infection, a wound complication, or another postpartum problem that needs medical assessment.

Pelvic girdle pain, which can be severe and affect walking and daily activities, sometimes continues after delivery rather than resolving immediately as many women expect. Lower back pain, pubic symphysis pain, and hip pain can all persist in the postpartum period and respond well to physiotherapy.

See a doctor if postpartum pain is severe, worsening, accompanied by fever, unusual discharge, or difficulty passing urine, or if pain is significantly limiting your ability to care for yourself and your baby after the first two weeks.

When to seek help: See a doctor if postpartum pain is severe, worsening, accompanied by fever or unusual discharge, or significantly limiting your ability to care for yourself and your baby.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Why Do I Feel So Emotional After Delivery?
answer:
My dear,

The dramatic hormonal shift after delivery, when oestrogen and progesterone levels that were very high during pregnancy fall sharply within hours of delivering the placenta, causes a period of emotional volatility in most new mothers. Tearfulness, anxiety, mood swings, and emotional sensitivity in the first few days are experienced by the majority of women and are called the baby blues.

Baby blues typically peak around day three or four after delivery and settle within a couple of weeks without specific treatment, though rest, support, and kind understanding from those around the new mother make a significant difference. They are a normal physiological response to dramatic hormonal change.

When these symptoms do not settle within two weeks, or when they are more severe, persistent, or significantly affecting the mother's ability to function or care for her baby, this may represent postnatal depression, which is a common and treatable medical condition affecting approximately one in seven new mothers.

See a doctor if emotional distress, persistent sadness, anxiety, or difficulty functioning continues beyond two weeks after delivery, or at any time if you are having thoughts of harming yourself or your baby.

When to seek help: See a doctor if low mood, anxiety, or emotional distress after delivery persists beyond two weeks, or at any time if thoughts of harming yourself or the baby are present.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: What Is Postnatal Depression and How Is It Different from Baby Blues?
answer:
My dear,

Postnatal depression is a depressive illness that begins after childbirth and affects approximately one in seven to ten new mothers. It is distinct from baby blues in its duration, severity, and impact. Baby blues are brief and self-resolving. Postnatal depression persists, deepens, and begins to affect the mother's ability to function, care for herself and her baby, and find joy in life.

Symptoms include persistent low mood, inability to feel pleasure in things that usually bring joy, overwhelming fatigue beyond normal new parent tiredness, constant anxiety, intrusive worrying about the baby's health or safety, difficulty sleeping even when the baby sleeps, changes in appetite, and sometimes distressing thoughts about the baby coming to harm.

Postnatal depression is not a reflection of love for the baby. A mother can be deeply in love with her baby and simultaneously experiencing postnatal depression. Both realities can coexist. It is not a character failing. It is a medical condition with neurobiological components that responds well to treatment including talking therapy and where needed medication that is safe during breastfeeding.

See a doctor if you recognise symptoms of postnatal depression in yourself or if someone close to you is concerned about how you are coping after delivery. Treatment is effective and you do not have to suffer alone.

When to seek help: See a doctor if symptoms of postnatal depression are present, including persistent low mood, anxiety, overwhelming fatigue, or intrusive worrying that is not settling within two weeks of delivery.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: How Long Should Postnatal Bleeding Last?
answer:
My dear,

Postnatal bleeding, called lochia, is normal after delivery and follows a predictable pattern. In the first few days, it is heavier and bright red, similar to a heavy period. Over the following days to weeks, it becomes lighter, pinker, then brownish, and then yellowish-white before stopping entirely. The total duration is typically two to six weeks.

Bleeding that becomes heavier rather than lighter, returns to bright red after it was settling, or is accompanied by large clots, fever, lower abdominal pain, or foul smell may indicate secondary postpartum haemorrhage, an infection, or retained placental tissue. Any of these requires prompt medical assessment.

Many women find that activity increases lochia temporarily, which is the body's way of communicating that it needs more rest. This is useful biological feedback rather than a cause for alarm, as long as the heavier flow settles with rest and is not accompanied by other concerning symptoms.

See a doctor if postnatal bleeding becomes heavier rather than lighter, returns after stopping, is accompanied by large clots, fever, foul smell, or lower abdominal pain, or continues beyond six weeks.

When to seek help: See a doctor if postnatal bleeding becomes heavier, returns, is accompanied by large clots, fever, foul smell, or lower abdominal pain, or continues beyond six weeks.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: When Can I Resume Intimate Closeness After Delivery?
answer:
My dear,

There is no single medically mandated date at which intimate closeness must or cannot resume after delivery. What matters most is the woman's own physical healing, her comfort, and her emotional readiness. The traditional advice of waiting six weeks is a guideline, not a fixed rule, and individual recovery varies significantly.

Physically, the perineum needs time to heal, the lochia needs to stop, and if stitches were placed, they need to have dissolved and the skin to have healed. Hormonally, particularly during breastfeeding, oestrogen levels remain low, causing vaginal dryness that makes closeness uncomfortable without appropriate lubrication.

Emotionally, a new mother's capacity for and interest in intimacy is often very different from her pre-pregnancy experience. This is normal, expected, and not a sign of diminished love for her partner. Communication about both partners' needs and patience with the pace of recovery is more important than any specific timeline.

See a doctor if intimate closeness after delivery is persistently painful, if dryness is significant, if stitches are causing ongoing discomfort, or if emotional readiness is absent weeks or months after delivery.

When to seek help: See a doctor if intimate closeness after delivery is persistently painful, dryness is significant, stitches are causing ongoing pain, or if emotional readiness is absent for weeks or months.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: How Can I Care for Stitches After Delivery?
answer:
My dear,

Perineal stitches after delivery dissolve on their own and do not need to be removed. Caring for them well in the days and weeks after delivery significantly reduces the risk of infection and supports comfortable healing. The primary principles are cleanliness, gentle drying, and pain management.

Rinsing the area with clean warm water after using the toilet and before and after changing pads helps keep the stitches clean without harsh scrubbing. Gently patting dry, rather than rubbing, protects the healing tissue. Changing pads frequently reduces moisture and bacteria accumulation. Air circulation, which can be achieved by lying down without tight underwear for short periods, supports healing.

Pain relief in the first days to weeks is important. Discomfort that prevents a new mother from sleeping, feeding her baby comfortably, or moving normally deserves adequate pain management rather than being endured. Adequate pain control helps recovery rather than hindering it.

See a doctor if the stitches area becomes increasingly red, swollen, hot, or painful, if there is discharge with a foul smell, if the wound appears to be opening, or if pain is not reducing after the first one to two weeks.

When to seek help: See a doctor if the perineal area is increasingly red, swollen, hot, or painful, if discharge smells foul, if the wound appears to open, or if pain is not improving after the first two weeks.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Why Do I Have Stool Pain or Problems After Delivery?
answer:
My dear,

Constipation and pain with opening the bowels are very common in the days after delivery. Several factors combine to cause this: the bowel has often slowed during labour, iron supplements taken for anaemia cause constipation, fear of pain around stitches causes women to hold the stool, and postnatal haemorrhoids, which are very common, add to the discomfort.

Straining hard with constipated stool on a healing perineum is painful and can put pressure on the stitches. Keeping stool soft is not a minor concern after delivery. It is an important part of perineal recovery. Adequate fluid intake, fibre from food, gentle mobilisation as soon as possible after delivery, and a stool softener if needed are all appropriate and helpful measures.

Haemorrhoids that developed during pregnancy or delivery often improve significantly in the weeks after birth as swelling reduces and bowel habits normalise. Cold compresses, soothing preparations, and avoiding constipation are the first-line approaches.

See a doctor if stool pain is severe, if bleeding from the back passage is significant, if the stool stays hard despite adequate fluid and fibre, or if haemorrhoids are severe and not responding to simple care.

When to seek help: See a doctor if stool pain is severe, bleeding from the back passage is significant, constipation persists despite adequate fluids and fibre, or haemorrhoids are severe.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Are Anal Problems After Delivery Anything to Feel Shy About Discussing?
answer:
My dear,

No. Pain, bleeding, growths, itching, or swelling near the back passage are medical concerns that deserve straightforward medical attention, exactly as any other health problem does. The fact that they occur in a private location does not make them shameful or embarrassing. Doctors who care for new mothers see these problems very regularly.

Haemorrhoids, anal fissures, skin tags, and other conditions affecting the anus and perineum after delivery are among the most common postpartum complaints and among the least often discussed. The silence around them means many women suffer longer than necessary when effective treatments are readily available.

Anal fissures, which are small tears in the skin of the anus, cause sharp pain during and after passing stool that can be so intense that the woman avoids opening her bowels, which worsens the constipation, which worsens the fissure. Breaking this cycle with stool softeners, topical treatments, and adequate pain relief is highly effective when treatment is sought.

See a doctor for any anal or perineal problem after delivery that is causing pain, bleeding, significant discomfort, or anxiety. These are medical problems that deserve care, not silent endurance.

When to seek help: See a doctor for any anal or perineal pain, bleeding, growths, or discomfort after delivery. These are medical concerns that deserve straightforward care, not silence.

With lots of love and care, Your Health Sakhi

question: Intimacy Before Marriage: What Are the Real Risks?
answer:
My dear,

This topic deserves honest information rather than either moral pressure or false reassurance. The physical risks of intimacy before marriage are the same as the physical risks at any other time: pregnancy and infections that spread through intimate contact. These risks do not disappear based on relationship status or personal intention.

A person can look completely healthy and carry an infection that has no symptoms. The only way to know is to test. Condoms used correctly and consistently from the beginning of any contact significantly reduce both pregnancy risk and the risk of most infections. They do not eliminate risk completely but they reduce it very substantially.

Emotional risks are also real. Intimacy in situations where there is unequal power, where one person feels pressured, where alcohol or other substances are involved, or where consent is unclear or incomplete creates the potential for emotional harm that may persist long after the physical encounter is over.

See a doctor if there was unprotected intimate contact, if a period is missed, or if you need guidance on contraception, testing, or support after an experience that did not feel safe or fully chosen.
